extracted.intended_audience: government contracting officers, procurement lawyers, contractors, sureties, and auditors handling U.S. federal contracts
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for interpreting and administering United States government contracts (set-offs, liquidated damages, bonds for labor and material, liens, retained percentages, withholdings, and related remedies). Compiles comptroller/administrative decisions and statutory interpretations relevant to settlements and withholding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-off: liquidated vs unliquidated amounts
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be set off against amounts due a contractor an amount due from him as damages under another contract provided the amount due from him is a liquidated amount; where the amount due from the contractor is not liquidated, the Government has no strict legal right to insist on set-off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the government itself has fixed the unliquidated amount as properly due, it still lacks a legal right of set-off but has an equitable right to withhold money in its discretion until the unliquidated claim can be adjusted in the Court of Claims, which has jurisdiction of all set-offs, counterclaims, claims for damages (liquidated or unliquidated). Examples: withholding to cover uncertain fresh-water charges or dredging losses is permitted as an equitable withholding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable right to withhold pending adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: Even absent a strict legal right of set-off for unliquidated claims, the Government has an equitable right to withhold money due (or to become due) to a contractor as security until the unliquidated claim can be judicially adjusted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withholding is discretionary and intended to protect public interest; advisable to refer unresolved amounts to Court of Claims or await judicial adjustment. Where a definite amount of damages has already accrued, it is a proper subject for set-off and may be retained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withholding not justified for private third-party claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The United States will not be justified in withholding payments to a contractor to compensate private claims belonging to third parties (e.g., private claims in favor of soldiers against ship owners).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish governmental losses (which may justify withholding) from private claims of third parties that do not authorize withholding of government payments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of bid does not automatically create debt under §3744
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance of a bidder's offer accompanied by a guaranty does not itself constitute a contract under section 3744, R.S., nor create a debt or obligation from the bidder where the bidder refuses to enter into the formal contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government's remedy is an action on the guaranty for loss (difference between the bid and subsequent contract price), not withholding payments due on unrelated contracts; cannot withhold other contract payments to compensate for bidder's refusal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erroneous overpayment recovery by set-off
rubrics_metrics.description: Where through mistake an officer failed to deduct liquidated damages that had accrued, there may be withheld from the contractor money due on another contract to reimburse the Government for the erroneous overpayment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government may correct mistakes by withholding to recoup amounts erroneously paid, subject to applicable rules and procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeiture clause ambiguity — treat as penalty when actual damages ascertainable (XIX A)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a contract provides for a forfeiture for delay but does not state whether sums forfeited are penalties or liquidated damages, and actual damages are capable of ascertainment, the forfeiture should be treated as a penalty and excess over actual damages should be remitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When actual damages can be determined, avoid enforcing a disproportionate forfeiture; treat the clause as penal and limit recovery to actual loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Price reduction clauses for delay are penalties when disproportionate (XIX B)
rubrics_metrics.description: A contractual provision reducing price for late delivery (e.g., deducting one-half of 1 per cent per day) is a penalty for delayed delivery when it is not a genuine pre-estimate of loss; contractor is entitled to full price less actual damages only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret price-reduction schedules skeptically if they function as punitive discounts rather than fair compensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeiture of retained percentages is a penalty (XIX C)
rubrics_metrics.description: A provision that on default all sums due or to become due and all retained percentages shall be forfeited to the United States is a penalty; on default the contractor is entitled to payment of withheld moneys beyond any actual damage sustained by the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retentions intended to secure completion should not be converted into punitive forfeitures; on default compute actual damage and release excess retained sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liquidated damages clause across multiple independent obligations construed as penalty (XIX D)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a contract requires doing two or more independent things (e.g., erecting multiple houses) and provides an entire-contract completion date with liquidated damages for delay, the clause will not be enforced as liquidated damages but construed as a penalty if the separate items are independent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not enforce aggregate liquidated damages where independent portions completed in time make an entire-contract forfeiture disproportionate; treat as penalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bid deposit forfeiture treated as penalty (XIX E)
rubrics_metrics.description: A required deposit (e.g., 20% certified check) accompanying bids, forfeited when highest bidder fails to complete purchase, is a penalty and should be returned less any actual damages sustained by reason of the failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contracting officers should assess actual damages before declaring deposits forfeited and return excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grossly excessive liquidated damages construed as penalty (XIX F)
rubrics_metrics.description: When liquidated damages are grossly in excess of likely actual damages, violating the principle that they represent a just compensation, the provision will be construed as a penalty and enforced only to the extent of actual damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show percentages up to and exceeding contract price; such excessive figures are penal unless special circumstances (urgent need, exigency) at contract formation justify them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual exceptions for high liquidated damages (XIX F exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where at contract making there was urgent need or special circumstances (e.g., Panama Canal machines), a high liquidated-damages rate may be upheld and not construed as a penalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider facts at formation: urgent public necessity or circumstances may validate higher liquidated damages as legitimate pre-estimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental contract deductions for actual additional expense (XIX G)
rubrics_metrics.description: A supplemental contract permitting deduction of any additional expense or loss incurred by the United States because of contractor failure (e.g., extension inspector salary/expenses) are actual damages, not penalties, and must be withheld in settlement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deductions for verifiable additional government expense caused by contractor delay are permissible as actual damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subcontractor delay not automatically an unforeseeable excuse (XIX H)
rubrics_metrics.description: A provision allowing additional time for 'unforeseeable cause of delay arising through no fault of the contractor' does not include tardy delivery of material by a subcontractor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contractors remain responsible for subcontractor performance unless contract expressly shifts that risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution purchases and damages for failure to deliver (XIX I)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where contractor fails to deliver specific supplies and government purchases substitutes, contractor is liable for any excess cost over contract prices; parties are presumed to have contemplated substitute purchases in breach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charge contractor with increased cost of reasonable substitute purchases when original goods unavailable; government should purchase reasonably equivalent items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of increased costs caused by other contractor's delay (XIX I1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If contractor A's failure forces increased cost or time for contractor B (e.g., plumbing delayed by building contractor), the additional cost to the United States should be charged against contractor A and his surety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hold primary defaulting contractors accountable for downstream increased costs due to their delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government may but is not required to complete contractor's work on default (XIX J)
rubrics_metrics.description: When work is largely incomplete and delayed, the United States may take charge and complete at the contractor's expense but is not required to do so; contract may be treated as abandoned and contractor/surety held liable for actual damages, with fresh contracts made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider abandonment and fresh contracting when partial performance is minimal and unreasonable extension would be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retained percentages secure completion; paid when government abandons work (XIX K)
rubrics_metrics.description: Retained percentages (e.g., 20%) are security for completion; if the government abandons the work and adopts a new system making damages impossible to ascertain, retained percentages for work already done should be paid to contractor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Release retained funds when government acts to abandon the contract making it impossible to ascertain loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractor liable for actual damages from failure to meet specification (XIX L)
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to comply strictly with contract specifications (e.g., hay density) makes contractor legally responsible for actual damages resulting therefrom (such as excess freight) which can be deducted at final settlement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforce strict compliance when specification failure causes verifiable government expense; compute and deduct actual damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay caused by other party before contractor can start — reasonable time allowed (XIX M/N)
rubrics_metrics.description: If contractor cannot commence because another contractor has failed to construct the building, contractor is not liable for damages for the period he was prevented from starting; after that, he is entitled to a reasonable time to complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish excused delay period (no liability) from subsequent performance window where reasonable time is expected; measure actual promptness thereafter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certified check cannot substitute for bond under Aug 13, 1894 (XX C3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the act of August 13, 1894, a certified check cannot be accepted in lieu of the contractor's bond required to secure payment to persons supplying labor and material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require the statutory bond rather than certified checks where the act applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory bond for labor and material — scope and liberal construction (XX C1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of August 13, 1894 requires a bond conditioned for payment to persons supplying 'labor and material' in construction of public buildings or prosecution/completion of public works; the remedial act should be liberally construed to apply where the contract involves prosecution/completion of public work, including dredging or wreck removal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contracting officers should generally exact the bond unless clearly outside statute's scope (e.g., work where title remains in contractor until acceptance). Applies to repairs on government-owned property where title remains in Government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute does not necessarily apply to contracts made and performed abroad (XX C2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the act does not expressly govern contracts made abroad and state laws don't operate beyond their borders, the statute is believed not to apply to a contract made and to be performed in a foreign country absent a stipulation to the contrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat foreign contracts as governed by applicable foreign law unless the contract states otherwise; if foreign law provides a lien, the U.S. acquisition may subject the United States to that lien.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit requirements for obtaining certified copy of bond (XX C4)
rubrics_metrics.description: The act requires a certified copy of the contractor's bond be furnished upon application accompanied by an affidavit; an affidavit 'upon information and belief' by an attorney or assignee is insufficient—affidavit should be of the party furnishing labor/material or someone with first-hand knowledge. Secretary of War may, however, furnish on less evidence at his discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow statutory affidavit standard when requesting bond copies; administrative discretion may relax strictness in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Furnishing copy of contract and bond after complete performance (XX C5)
rubrics_metrics.description: When bond given under the act has been completely performed so there will be no suit by the United States, a copy of the contract and bond should be furnished upon proper application without waiting six months from completion and final settlement (final settlement by auditor). If suit has been brought by Government, copies should not be furnished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish completed, settled contracts from those subject to government suit in deciding disclosure of bond/contract copies.

rubrics_metrics.name: New surety obligation under statute confers no equitable lien on United States (XX C6)
rubrics_metrics.description: The surety's new obligation under the act of Aug 13, 1894 does not create any additional right against the United States (e.g., equitable lien); the United States has no right to withhold funds due a contractor for the purpose of indemnifying a surety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not withhold contractor payments at surety's request to indemnify the surety; government should not assume obligations to insure surety payments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modification of contract without surety consent does not release surety's obligation to labor/material-men (XX C7)
rubrics_metrics.description: A contractor's bond under the act may be considered two obligations; the obligation for the benefit of labor and material-men is not released by modification of the contract without surety consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labor and material-men retain rights under the bond despite government-contractor modifications absent surety consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contracts with municipal instrumentalities — doubt about statute coverage (XX C8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contracts made with municipal instrumentalities (e.g., board of water commissioners) may be doubtful fits under the act; recommended practice is not to exact the bond for protection of persons supplying labor and materials in such doubtful cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise caution and consider statutory intent before demanding bond for contracts with municipal entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative remedies not to be used to coerce surety settlement (XX C9)
rubrics_metrics.description: The War Department's striking a surety company from its list of acceptable companies to compel settlement with a subcontractor is outside the department's duty under the act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use debarment/lists as substitute for statutory remedies; follow statutory procedures for enforcement against sureties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on subcontractor liens against United States property (XX A/B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subcontractors/ material-men generally may not enforce mechanic's or material-man's liens against United States property or instrumentality (including D.C. and soldiers' homes); recognizing such a lien would amount to sanctioning an indirect transfer of interest in the contract, contrary to sec. 3737 Rev. Stat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State lien remedies that require suing a State tribunal in rem are often inapplicable against the United States; public policy bars obstructing federal functions by state process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary of War cannot consent to suit by subcontractors against surety in name of U.S. without legislative authority (XX B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where contract covenants make the contractor responsible for labor/material liabilities, the Secretary cannot legally consent to subcontractors suing the sureties in the name of the United States for their own use; such consent would part with a right of action of the United States without congressional authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedies for subcontractor claims against sureties require statutory authority; contracting covenants give the U.S. remedies in damages but do not authorize substitutionary suits by subcontractors absent legislation.
